answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.4.2024) The investigation of radio frequency interferences is a competence of the Member States. The Commission monitors the performance and potential impact on the use of the European Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS): Galileo and European Geostationary Navigation Overlay Service (EGNOS).
The Commission has initiated activities to have a regular monitoring of interference to Galileo and EGNOS signals with the potential to localise the sources of interference.

The Commission has contributed to resolutions by the International Telecommunication Union1, the International Civil Aviation Organization2 and the EU Aviation Safety Agency (EASA)3 which request countries to monitor, localise and stop the sources of interference. Intentional jamming or spoofing of GNSS belong to the counterspace capabilities developed by some third countries.

This is one of the space threats, which the EU addresses as part of its new Space Strategy for Security and Defence4. The Strategy acknowledges that space is a strategic domain and proposes a set of measures to enhance the resilience and protection of space systems and services in the Member States.

In this context, the Navguard project5 financed by the European Defence Fund will develop ground and space-based systems to detect illegitimate activities in Galileo frequency bands and geolocate the sources of malicious activities.

EASA published a bulletin6 for national aviation authorities, air navigation service providers and aircraft operators recommending to develop contingency plans with the procedures to be followed in case of such large-scale events.

EUROCONTROL published guidance7 to develop these contingency plans, and it works with all operational stakeholders on a minimal operational network of terrestrial conventional systems to be maintained to ensure safety in case of GNSS interferences. A crisis exercise is planned to help define mitigation measures and contingency plans.
The Member States, under the coordination of the Commission, have raised the growing safety concern about GNSS interferences at the level of the United Nations.
